questions.text: What happens to the space of a logical volume after lvremove /dev/TEST/vol_name_1?
options: It is lost until the disk is repartitioned
It returns to the volume group as free space
It is moved to a snapshot automatically
It becomes a new physical volume
questions.explanation: Removing an LV frees its extents in the VG, which vgs shows as VFree. Unmount the LV first, and remember its data is gone.

questions.text: How does an LVM snapshot preserve the original state of a logical volume?
options: It copies the whole LV when the snapshot is created
It uses copy-on-write, keeping old blocks only as they change on the origin
It compresses the origin LV into a file
It mirrors all writes to a second disk
questions.explanation: A new snapshot is nearly empty. When a block on the origin is about to change, the old block is saved into the snapshot, so it only needs space for changed data.

questions.text: Which command creates a 1 GB snapshot named snap1 of /dev/TEST/vol_name_1?
questions.explanation: lvcreate -s makes a snapshot of the origin LV, with -L reserving space for changed blocks. lvconvert --merge is used later to roll back to a snapshot.

questions.text: In lvs output, a snapshot's Data% reaches 100%. What does that mean?
options: The snapshot has been merged automatically
The snapshot ran out of space and is no longer valid
The snapshot is ready to be mounted
questions.explanation: Once the snapshot's space is used up by changed blocks, it can no longer represent the earlier state and becomes invalid. Extend or remove snapshots before they fill, and do not keep them longer than needed.

questions.text: A risky upgrade broke the data on /dev/TEST/vol_name_1, which has the snapshot snap1. Which command rolls the LV back to the snapshot?
questions.explanation: Merging writes the snapshot's preserved state back into the origin. If the origin is in use, the merge happens at the next activation, so unmount it first.

questions.text: Why are LVM snapshots not a replacement for real backups?
options: Snapshots are deleted at every reboot
Snapshots only store file names, not data
Snapshots live on the same storage, so a disk failure can destroy them along with the origin
questions.explanation: A snapshot depends on the origin LV and sits in the same volume group. Keep separate backups on other storage for disaster recovery.

questions.text: After booting a rescue system, lvs lists your logical volumes but they cannot be mounted because they are inactive. Which command activates them?
questions.explanation: vgchange -ay activates all logical volumes in all volume groups, creating their device nodes. Check with lsblk afterwards, then mount them.

questions.text: Why must you be careful running pvcreate /dev/sdb?
options: It writes LVM metadata to the disk and destroys any data already on it
It removes the disk from all volume groups
It changes the disk's device name
questions.explanation: pvcreate initializes the device for LVM, overwriting what was there. Confirm the device with lsblk before running it.

questions.text: In a typical Linux server layout that uses LVM, which part is usually kept as a plain partition rather than a logical volume?
questions.explanation: Firmware must read the EFI system partition (and often /boot) directly, without LVM support, so they stay plain partitions. /, /home and /var benefit from LVM's resizing.

questions.text: Which command prints a one-time snapshot of every process on the system, with user, PID, CPU and memory columns?
questions.explanation: ps aux lists all processes for all users with %CPU, %MEM, STAT and the command. Plain ps shows only processes on the current terminal, top is a live view, and jobs lists only the current shell's jobs.

questions.text: Which ps option selects every process on the system in standard (UNIX) syntax, as in ps -ef?
questions.explanation: -e (same as -A) selects all processes, and -f adds full-format columns such as UID, PPID and start time. -a omits session leaders and processes without a terminal, -u filters by user and -p by PID.

questions.text: Which command lists only the processes owned by the user alice?
questions.explanation: ps -u alice selects processes by effective user. pgrep -u alice gives just their PIDs. -p expects PIDs, not user names.

questions.text: Which command prints only the parent PID of process 1234, with no header line?
questions.explanation: -o ppid= selects the PPID column and the trailing = removes its header; -p 1234 picks the process. pgrep -P 1234 does the reverse: it lists the children of 1234.

questions.text: Which command shows processes as a tree, making parent-child relationships easy to see?
questions.explanation: pstree draws the process hierarchy, and -p adds PIDs. ps fax gives a similar ASCII-art tree. ps aux and pgrep -l print flat lists.

questions.text: Which command prints the PIDs and names of all running processes called nginx?
questions.explanation: pgrep matches process names and prints PIDs; -l adds the name. Add -f to match against the full command line, -u user to filter by owner, or -n for the newest match.

questions.text: Why does ps -ef | grep firefox often include an extra line that is not Firefox?
options: ps lists each Firefox thread as a separate process
The grep firefox process itself matches the pattern
ps -ef prints a header line containing the search term
Firefox starts a watchdog process with the same name
questions.explanation: The grep process's own command line contains firefox, so it matches. Use grep '[f]irefox', add grep -v grep, or switch to pgrep firefox.

questions.text: Which command gives a continuously updating view of processes, sorted by CPU usage by default?
questions.explanation: top refreshes every few seconds and shows a system summary (load, CPU, memory) above the process list. ps prints a single snapshot.

questions.text: While top is running, which key sorts the process list by memory usage?
questions.explanation: M sorts by %MEM and P sorts by %CPU. k prompts for a PID to signal, and r renices a process.

questions.text: In htop, what is the difference between pressing F4 and F3?
options: F4 kills the selected process and F3 stops it
F4 filters out non-matching rows and F3 searches while keeping every row
F4 sorts by memory and F3 sorts by CPU
F4 shows threads and F3 hides them
questions.explanation: F4 (Filter) hides processes that do not match the typed text, and F3 (Search) jumps to matches without hiding anything else. F9 sends a signal and F6 changes the sort column.

questions.text: What is PID 1 on a systemd-based distribution?
options: systemd, the first user-space process, which starts services and adopts orphans
The login shell of the first user to log in
kthreadd, the parent of every process
questions.explanation: The kernel starts PID 1 (systemd or init), which brings up the user-space service tree and normally adopts orphaned processes. Kernel threads descend from kthreadd (PID 2), not from PID 1.

questions.text: In C, what does fork() do?
options: Replaces the current program with a new one while keeping the PID
Creates a new child process that is a copy of the calling process
Waits for a child process to exit and collects its status
Sends a signal to another process
questions.explanation: fork() returns twice: 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent. Replacing the program image is the exec family, and collecting exit status is wait()/waitpid().

questions.text: A child process calls execl("/bin/ls", "ls", (char *)NULL) and it succeeds. What happens to the child's PID?
options: The kernel assigns a new PID for ls
It stays the same, because exec replaces the program in the same process
It becomes 1, because exec re-parents the process to init
questions.explanation: The exec family loads a new program image into the existing process; no new process is created. That is why shells use fork() first, then exec in the child.

questions.text: What is the main difference between a process and a thread?
options: Threads always run on a different CPU core from their process
Each process has its own address space, while threads in one process share memory
A process can contain only one thread at a time
Threads have their own PIDs and memory, while processes share memory
questions.explanation: Threads of one process share the same memory and open files but have separate stacks and registers. ps -eLo pid,tid,stat,comm lists threads with their thread IDs (TID).

questions.text: Which command sends SIGTERM, asking process 1234 to shut down cleanly?
questions.explanation: kill sends SIGTERM (15) by default, which a program may catch to clean up. -9 is SIGKILL, -STOP pauses the process, and signal 0 only checks whether the PID exists.

questions.text: Which signal cannot be caught, blocked or ignored, and so ends a process immediately?
questions.explanation: The kernel handles SIGKILL (9) itself, so the program cannot run cleanup code. Use it only after SIGTERM fails. SIGSTOP is likewise uncatchable, but it pauses the process instead of killing it.

questions.text: What happens when you press Ctrl+C while a command runs in the foreground?
options: The terminal sends SIGKILL to the command
The terminal sends SIGINT to the foreground process group
The shell sends SIGTSTP and parks the job
The terminal sends SIGHUP and closes the session
questions.explanation: Ctrl+C generates SIGINT (2), an interrupt that programs may catch. Ctrl+Z generates SIGTSTP, which stops the job instead of ending it.

questions.text: Which command terminates every process named firefox without looking up PIDs first?
questions.explanation: pkill matches processes by name (like pgrep) and sends them a signal, SIGTERM by default. kill expects PIDs or job specs such as %1, not names.

questions.text: How can you pause process 1234 and later let it continue from where it stopped?
questions.explanation: kill -STOP 1234 freezes the process (state T), and kill -CONT 1234 resumes it. SIGSTOP cannot be caught or ignored. A killed process cannot be continued.

questions.text: Many daemons, such as nginx, do what when they receive SIGHUP?
options: Reload their configuration files without a full restart
Dump their memory to a core file
questions.explanation: SIGHUP originally meant "terminal hung up", and its default action is to terminate. Many daemons have no terminal, so they catch it and treat it as a request to reload configuration.

questions.text: What does kill -s TERM -- -2345 do?
options: Sends SIGTERM to the process with PID 2345
Sends SIGTERM to every process in process group 2345
Sends SIGTERM to every process the user may signal
Sends SIGTERM to process 2345 and its parent
questions.explanation: A negative target (other than -1) means a process group, and -- stops kill from reading -2345 as an option. Target -1 means all processes you may signal, and 0 means your own process group.

questions.text: How do you start ./backup.sh so that it runs in the background and you get the prompt back immediately?
questions.explanation: A trailing & starts the command as a background job and prints its job number and PID, such as [1] 3241. bg resumes an existing stopped job, and nohup alone still runs the command in the foreground.

questions.text: You press Ctrl+Z while long_task.sh runs in the foreground. What state is the job in afterwards?
options: Stopped, until you resume it with fg or bg
Terminated, with its exit status saved
Still running in the foreground, but with output hidden
questions.explanation: Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP, which stops (pauses) the job and returns the prompt. bg resumes it in the background and fg brings it back to the foreground.

questions.text: Which command brings job number 2 back to the foreground?
questions.explanation: %2 is a job spec for job 2 in this shell. bg %2 resumes it in the background instead, and kill -CONT 2 would target PID 2, not job 2.

questions.text:
In this jobs -l output, what does the + mean?

[1]  + 3241 Running    sleep 1000 &
[2]  - 3250 Stopped    vi notes.txt
options: Job 1 has a higher scheduling priority
Job 1 is the current job, used by fg and bg when no job is named
Job 1 has finished and is waiting to be cleared
questions.explanation: + marks the current job and - the previous one. Plain fg or bg acts on the + job.

questions.text: In a script, what does the wait builtin do?
options: Sleeps for a fixed number of seconds
Blocks until the script's background child processes have finished
Waits for the user to press Enter
Suspends the script until it receives SIGCONT
questions.explanation: wait with no arguments waits for all background children; wait PID waits for one and returns its exit status. Pausing for a duration is sleep.

questions.text: You start ./long_job.sh & over SSH, and the job dies when you log out. Which change keeps it running after logout?
questions.explanation: Closing the session sends SIGHUP to its jobs. nohup makes the command ignore SIGHUP; redirecting alone does not, it only avoids writing to a closed terminal. For critical work, a service manager, tmux or screen is better.

questions.text: What range of nice values does Linux use, and which end gets the most CPU time?
questions.explanation: Lower nice values mean higher priority, so -20 is the least "nice" to other processes. The default is 0, and ordinary users may only raise a value (lower the priority).

questions.text: Which command starts make with lower CPU priority so it does not slow down interactive work?
questions.explanation: nice -n 10 starts a new command with niceness 10, which is lower priority. A negative value raises priority and needs root. renice changes an already-running process and takes a PID, not a command.

questions.text: Which command changes the priority of the running process 4321 to niceness 5?
questions.explanation: renice adjusts existing processes by PID (-p), group or user. nice only launches new commands, so nice -n 5 4321 would try to run a program called 4321.

questions.text: What is a zombie process (state Z)?
options: A process stuck in uninterruptible disk I/O
A child that has exited but whose parent has not yet collected its exit status
A process that has been stopped with SIGSTOP
A process whose parent died and that was adopted by PID 1
questions.explanation: A zombie has finished running and holds only a process-table entry until its parent calls wait(). Waiting on disk I/O is state D, stopped is T, and an adopted process is an orphan, not a zombie.

questions.text: ps keeps showing a zombie child of PID 800, even after kill -9 on the zombie. What actually removes it?
options: Sending SIGKILL again with kill -s KILL
Having PID 800 reap it with wait(), or ending PID 800 so PID 1 adopts and reaps it
questions.explanation: A zombie has already exited, so there is nothing left for a signal to kill. Only reaping removes the entry: fix or restart the parent, and if the parent dies, PID 1 adopts and reaps the zombie.

questions.text: Many processes sit in state D for a long time while vmstat shows high wa. What does this suggest?
options: A CPU bottleneck from compute-heavy threads
An I/O bottleneck, such as a slow disk or a stuck network filesystem
A parent process that is not reaping its children
Processes that were stopped with Ctrl+Z
questions.explanation: D is uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting on kernel I/O, and such tasks often cannot be killed until the I/O finishes. Many R tasks point to CPU pressure, many Z to a broken parent, and T to stopped jobs.

questions.text: In ps -eo pid,stat,comm output, what does a STAT value of S mean?
options: The process is stopped and must be resumed with SIGCONT
The process is in interruptible sleep, waiting for an event such as input or a timer
The process is a session leader and is currently running
The process is swapped out to disk
questions.explanation: S means interruptible sleep, which is normal for most processes most of the time. A trailing s (as in Ss) marks a session leader, + the foreground group, and l a multi-threaded process.

questions.text: Which command shows the 1-, 5- and 15-minute load averages, along with uptime and logged-in user count?
questions.explanation: uptime prints a line such as up 1 day, 2 users, load average: 0.42, 0.35, 0.30. The same figures appear in the first line of top.

questions.text: A 4-core server shows a load average of 6.80, 4.10, 2.30, but CPU usage is low and vmstat shows high b and wa. What is driving the load?
options: Tasks blocked on I/O, which Linux also counts in the load average
Too much free memory being cached
Zombie processes using up CPU time
questions.explanation: Linux load counts runnable tasks and tasks in uninterruptible (D) sleep, so I/O waits raise it even when the CPU is idle. High b (blocked) and wa (I/O wait) confirm the cause. Zombies use no CPU.

questions.text: What is a daemon?
options: A process that has crashed and left a core dump
A background service process, such as one that handles logging, printing or networking
Any process started from a terminal with &
A process that runs only as root
questions.explanation: Daemons provide services in the background and are usually started at boot or on demand by a service manager. Many run under dedicated unprivileged accounts, and a shell job started with & is still a shell job.

questions.text: Which command lists every thread of every process, with a thread ID column?
questions.explanation: -L shows one row per thread, and tid is the thread ID. Threads of one process share its PID but have their own TIDs and states, which helps spot the one thread using CPU.

questions.text: In a shell with background jobs, what is the difference between kill %1 and kill 1?
options: They are the same; % is optional
kill %1 signals job number 1 in this shell, while kill 1 targets the process with PID 1
kill %1 sends SIGKILL, while kill 1 sends SIGTERM
kill %1 signals the first process listed by ps
questions.explanation: %N is a job spec that the shell translates into the job's processes. A plain number is a PID, and PID 1 is systemd or init, which ordinary users are not allowed to signal.

questions.text: ps -o pid,stat,comm -p 3250 shows STAT as T. What does that mean?
options: The process is a kernel thread
The process is stopped, for example by Ctrl+Z, SIGSTOP or a debugger
The process is terminating and will exit shortly
The process is waiting on a TCP connection
questions.explanation: T means stopped: the process does not run until it gets SIGCONT, for example from fg or bg. Exited processes that have not been reaped show Z.

questions.text: What is the difference between a terminal and a shell?
options: They are two names for the same program
The terminal is the window you type into; the shell interprets the commands
The shell draws the window; the terminal runs the commands
A terminal is used only for remote sessions, a shell only for local ones
questions.explanation: A terminal emulator such as GNOME Terminal or xterm provides the window and keyboard input. The shell (Bash, Zsh, and so on) runs inside it, parses commands and starts programs.

questions.text: Which file lists the shells that may be used as login shells, and is checked by chsh?
questions.explanation: chsh -s /bin/zsh normally refuses a shell that is not listed in /etc/shells. Each user's chosen login shell is then stored in the last field of their /etc/passwd entry.

questions.text: Your login shell is Bash, but you have just typed zsh to try it out. Which command reliably shows the shell you are running right now?
questions.explanation: $$ is the PID of the current shell, and ps prints its command name. $SHELL normally holds your default login shell, so it would still say /bin/bash.

questions.text: echo "$0" prints -bash. What does the leading dash tell you?
options: The shell is running in POSIX compatibility mode
The shell was started as a login shell
The shell is a non-interactive subshell
The shell is running with restricted permissions
questions.explanation: By convention, a login shell's argv[0] starts with -. Login shells read /etc/profile and then the first of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login or ~/.profile that exists.

questions.text: You log in over SSH, and Bash starts as a login shell. A user has both ~/.bash_profile and ~/.profile. Which files does Bash read?
questions.explanation: A login shell reads /etc/profile, then only the first user file it finds out of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login and ~/.profile. Here ~/.profile is skipped because ~/.bash_profile exists.

questions.text: Which file does Bash read when you open a new terminal tab in a desktop session (an interactive, non-login shell)?
questions.explanation: Interactive non-login shells read ~/.bashrc, often after a system-wide file such as /etc/bash.bashrc. Aliases, functions and prompt settings usually live there.

questions.text: Aliases defined in ~/.bashrc are missing when you log in over SSH. What is the usual fix?
options: Add export in front of each alias
questions.explanation: SSH starts a login shell, which reads ~/.bash_profile rather than ~/.bashrc. Adding if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then . ~/.bashrc; fi to ~/.bash_profile gives both kinds of shell the same settings.

questions.text: Which file does Bash run when a login shell exits?
questions.explanation: ~/.bash_logout runs when a login shell exits, which makes it handy for cleanup such as clearing the screen.

questions.text: You edited ~/.bashrc to add an alias. How do you apply it to the current shell without opening a new terminal?
questions.explanation: source (or .) runs the file inside the current shell, so its aliases and variables stay defined. bash ~/.bashrc runs it in a child process whose changes vanish when it exits.

questions.text:
A script run with bash exports a new value. What does the parent shell print afterwards?

export TOKEN=old
cat > change.sh <<'EOF'
export TOKEN=new
EOF
bash change.sh
echo "$TOKEN"
questions.explanation: bash change.sh runs in a child process. A child gets a copy of the parent's environment and cannot change the parent's copy. Using source change.sh would print new.

questions.text: Why must a Python virtual environment be activated with source venv/bin/activate, not by running ./venv/bin/activate?
options: The activate file is not marked executable
It must change PATH in the current shell, which a child process cannot do
Running it directly would install packages globally
source gives the script root privileges
questions.explanation: activate works by changing variables such as PATH and VIRTUAL_ENV. Only code that runs in the current shell, by being sourced, can change that shell's environment.

questions.text:
What does this print, given the difference between ( ) and { }?

COLOR=blue
( COLOR=red )
echo "$COLOR"
{ COLOR=green; }
echo "$COLOR"
questions.explanation: Parentheses run commands in a subshell, so its assignment is lost. Braces group commands in the current shell, so green sticks. Braces need spaces and a trailing ; before }.

questions.text:
What does printenv show for a variable that was set but never exported?

count=5
printenv count
options: It prints nothing, because count is a shell variable that was not exported
It fails with a syntax error
questions.explanation: printenv is an external program and sees only exported variables. Run export count first. echo "$count" would still print 5, because the shell expands the variable itself.

questions.text: What does DEBUG=1 ./app do?
options: Sets DEBUG permanently in the current shell and runs ./app
Puts DEBUG=1 in the environment of ./app only
Runs ./app with debug tracing turned on in Bash
questions.explanation: A NAME=value prefix adds the variable to that one command's environment. Afterwards echo "$DEBUG" in the shell prints nothing.

questions.text: Which line adds ~/bin to the front of the command search path for this shell and its children?
questions.explanation: PATH entries are separated by colons and searched left to right, so prepending puts ~/bin first. PATH=~/bin throws away the existing directories, and ; is not a separator on Linux.

questions.text: What does env -i bash --norc give you?
options: A Bash shell that runs as root
A new Bash process with an empty environment
A copy of the current shell, including its unexported variables
A Bash shell that ignores PATH lookups
questions.explanation: env -i clears the environment before starting the command. This is useful for checking whether a script secretly depends on your personal variables.

questions.text: What does readonly MAX_RETRIES=5 followed by MAX_RETRIES=3 do?
options: Changes the value to 3 and prints a warning
Changes the value to 3 only in child processes
questions.explanation: Read-only variables cannot be reassigned or unset in that shell, so Bash reports an error. This is useful for constants in scripts.

questions.text: A script starts with : "${API_KEY:?API_KEY is required}". What happens if API_KEY is unset?
options: API_KEY is set to the text API_KEY is required
The script prints the message to stderr and exits with a non-zero status
The line is ignored, because : is a comment
The script prompts the user to type a value
questions.explanation: ${VAR:?msg} aborts a non-interactive shell with msg if VAR is unset or empty. : is a no-op command that still expands its arguments, so the check runs.

questions.text:
What does this print when using the ${x:-7} default-value expansion?

x=5; echo "${x:-7}"; unset x; echo "${x:-7}"
questions.explanation: ${x:-7} uses the default 7 only when x is unset or empty, and does not assign it. The ${x:=7} form would also store 7 in x.

questions.text: Which shebang finds bash through the user's PATH, so the script works where Bash is not at /bin/bash?
questions.explanation: env searches PATH for bash, which helps on systems such as FreeBSD or macOS with Homebrew. #!/bin/sh may be Dash, which lacks Bash features. A shebang needs #! followed by the interpreter's full path.

questions.text: A script deploy.sh has a valid shebang. What lets you run it as ./deploy.sh?
questions.explanation: The kernel will only execve the file if it has execute permission; it then reads the shebang to pick the interpreter. bash deploy.sh runs the script without needing +x, but that is not ./deploy.sh.

questions.text: A script is run as ./greet.sh Ann Bob. Inside it, what are $0, $1 and $#?
questions.explanation: $0 is the name the script was invoked by, $1 is the first argument, and $# counts the arguments, not including $0.

questions.text:
What does this print, comparing "$@" with "$*"?

count() { echo "$#"; }
set -- "a b" c
count "$@"; count "$*"
questions.explanation: "$@" expands to each argument as a separate word, keeping a b intact, so you get 2. "$*" joins every argument into one string, so you get 1. Use "$@" to pass arguments through safely.

questions.text: What do $?, $$ and $! hold?
options: The PID of the last background job, the exit status, and the shell's PID
The last command's exit status, the current shell's PID, and the PID of the last background job
The argument count, the shell's PID, and the last exit status
The current shell's PID, the parent's PID, and the last exit status
questions.explanation: $? is 0 on success and non-zero on failure. $$ is the shell's own PID, and $! is set when you start something with &, which makes it useful with wait "$!".

questions.text: What does echo "Today is $(date +%A)" do?
options: Runs date +%A and puts its output into the string
Stores the output of date in a variable called A
questions.explanation: $(...) is command substitution: the command's stdout, without trailing newlines, replaces the expression. Backticks do the same thing but are harder to nest.

questions.text: With name=World, what does echo 'Hello $name' print?
questions.explanation: Single quotes keep every character literal. Double quotes, as in "Hello $name", still expand variables and command substitutions but prevent word splitting and globbing.

questions.text: Which alias definition makes ll run ls -la?
questions.explanation: There must be no spaces around =, and the value needs quotes because it contains a space. alias with no arguments lists all aliases, and unalias ll removes one.

questions.text: You want a shortcut backup notes.txt that copies a file to notes.txt.bak. Why use a function instead of an alias?
options: Aliases cannot contain the cp command
A function can use its argument as $1 anywhere in its body
Functions run faster because they are compiled
Aliases are deleted when the terminal is resized
questions.explanation: An alias is only text substitution at the start of a command, so it cannot reuse an argument. backup() { cp -- "$1" "$1.bak"; } can. Use aliases for simple shortcuts and functions for logic.

questions.text: Which of these is a valid Bash function definition?
questions.explanation: The body is a brace group, which needs a space after { and a ; or newline before }. Without the semicolon, Bash keeps reading and reports a syntax error.

questions.text: In PS1='\u@\h:\w\$ ', what do \u, \h and \w expand to?
options: User ID, home directory, and time
Username, hostname, and current working directory
Uptime, history number, and window title
Username, home directory, and week day
questions.explanation: PS1 is the primary prompt. \$ shows $ for normal users and # for root.

questions.text: What is the difference between HISTSIZE and HISTFILESIZE?
options: They are aliases for the same setting
HISTSIZE limits commands kept in memory; HISTFILESIZE limits lines saved in ~/.bash_history
HISTSIZE is in kilobytes; HISTFILESIZE is in lines
HISTSIZE applies to root; HISTFILESIZE applies to normal users
questions.explanation: During a session, Bash keeps up to HISTSIZE commands. When the shell exits, the history file is cut down to HISTFILESIZE lines.

questions.text: In an interactive Bash shell, what does sudo !! do?
options: Runs sudo with no arguments twice
Re-runs the previous command with sudo in front
Opens the history list in an editor
Repeats the last command that used sudo
questions.explanation: !! is history expansion for the previous command line. !$ expands to the last argument of the previous command.

questions.text: Which redirection sends both stdout and stderr of make to build.log, overwriting the file?
questions.explanation: Redirections are processed left to right: stdout goes to the file, then stderr is pointed at the same place. 2>&1 > build.log points stderr at the old stdout (the terminal) first. Bash's &> build.log is a shorter form.

questions.text: Which command adds a line to the end of notes.txt instead of replacing its contents?
questions.explanation: >> appends, while > truncates the file first. < redirects input, and 2> redirects only stderr.

questions.text: How do you run find / -name core and throw away its "Permission denied" messages, while still seeing the results?
questions.explanation: Error messages go to file descriptor 2, so 2>/dev/null discards just those. > /dev/null would discard the results, and &> would discard both streams.

questions.text: Which command shows output on screen and also appends it to run.log?
questions.explanation: tee copies stdin to the screen and to a file, and -a appends instead of overwriting. The redirect-only versions show nothing on screen.

questions.text:
What does this here-document print when its delimiter is quoted?

name=World
cat <<'EOF'
Hello $name
EOF
options: It fails because the delimiter is quoted
questions.explanation: Quoting the here-document delimiter ('EOF') turns off expansion in the body. With an unquoted EOF, the shell would expand $name and print Hello World.

questions.text: What does diff <(ls dir1) <(ls dir2) do?
options: Compares two files literally named ls dir1 and ls dir2
Compares the outputs of the two ls commands as if they were files
Copies dir1 into dir2, then compares them
Fails, because diff cannot read from pipes
questions.explanation: Process substitution <(cmd) runs the command and passes a path such as /dev/fd/63 that reads its output. That lets programs that expect filenames read command output.

questions.text: What does set -e change in a script?
options: It echoes each command before running it
The script exits when a command fails, outside tests such as if or &&
It exports every variable to child processes
It makes unset variables an error
questions.explanation: set -e (errexit) stops the script at the first unchecked failure. Commands used as conditions are exempt. Tracing is set -x, and unset-variable errors are set -u.

questions.text:
What does this script do when it uses an unset variable?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
echo "Count is $count"
echo "after"
options: An error like count: unbound variable, and the script stops
questions.explanation: set -u (nounset) makes expanding an unset variable an error, which ends a non-interactive shell. Without it, $count silently becomes an empty string and hides the bug.

questions.text:
What does this print, before and after enabling pipefail?

false | true; echo $?
set -o pipefail
false | true; echo $?
questions.explanation: A pipeline's status is normally that of its last command, so the failing false is hidden. With pipefail, a pipeline fails if any command in it fails.

questions.text: Which line is the usual "strict mode" at the top of a Bash script: exit on error, error on unset variables, and fail pipelines on any error?
questions.explanation: -e exits on unchecked errors, -u treats unset variables as errors, and -o pipefail makes pipeline failures visible. A + prefix turns options off instead of on.

questions.text: What does set -x do?
options: Exits the script on the first error
Prints each command, after expansion, before it runs
questions.explanation: set -x (xtrace) prints each command to stderr with a + prefix, which is useful for debugging. Turn it off again with set +x.

questions.text:
What does this trap line do in a script?

tmp=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT
options: Removes the temporary file whenever the script exits, including after an error
Stops the script from being interrupted with Ctrl+C
Prevents other users from reading the temporary file
questions.explanation: trap COMMAND EXIT runs the command when the shell exits for any reason. trap can also handle signals such as INT or TERM, which makes it the standard cleanup tool.

questions.text: Which command connects to server.example.com as user deploy?
questions.explanation: The form is ssh user@host. The equivalent option form is ssh -l deploy server.example.com; ssh has no -u or -user option.

questions.text: How do you run df -h on server and see its output locally, without opening an interactive shell?
questions.explanation: A command after the host runs on the remote side, and its output comes back to your terminal. In ssh user@server; df -h the df runs locally after the session ends, and -N runs no command at all.

questions.text: The SSH server listens on port 2222. Which command connects to it?
questions.explanation: ssh takes a lowercase -p for the port. scp and sftp use uppercase -P because their -p means "preserve times and modes". user@host:2222 is not port syntax for ssh.

questions.text: Which command generates a new Ed25519 key pair, the modern default choice for SSH keys?
questions.explanation: ssh-keygen -t TYPE creates a key pair, by default ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 and id_ed25519.pub. Ed25519 keys are short, fast and secure; for RSA, use at least 2048 bits with -b.

questions.text: After running ssh-keygen -t ed25519, which file must stay secret?
questions.explanation: The file without .pub is the private key; anyone holding it can log in as you wherever the public key is trusted. The .pub file is meant to be copied to servers.

questions.text: Which command installs your public key on a server so that later logins can use key authentication?
questions.explanation: ssh-copy-id appends the public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server, creating it if needed. Copying the private key, as in the scp option, defeats the point of key pairs.

questions.text: On the server, which file lists the public keys allowed to log in to a user account?
questions.explanation: sshd checks the target user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys during public-key authentication. known_hosts is the client's record of server host keys.

questions.text: During public-key authentication, what does the client send to prove its identity?
options: The private key, encrypted with the server's public key
A signature made with the private key, which the server checks against the public key
The user's password, hashed with the private key
The public key alone, with no further proof
questions.explanation: The private key never leaves the client. The server verifies the signature using the public key in authorized_keys, all inside the already-encrypted session.

questions.text: ssh refuses to use your key and warns UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE!. Which command fixes it?
questions.explanation: OpenSSH ignores private keys that other users can read. Mode 600 limits the file to its owner. The ~/.ssh directory itself is normally 700.

questions.text: Which option tells ssh to use a specific private key file?
questions.explanation: -i selects the identity (private key) file. -f sends ssh to the background, and -p sets the port.

questions.text: What does ssh-agent do?
options: It generates new key pairs on demand
It holds decrypted private keys in memory so you enter each passphrase only once
It runs on the server and checks authorized_keys
It copies public keys to remote servers
questions.explanation: The agent keeps unlocked keys in memory and answers signing requests from ssh. You add keys to it with ssh-add. The server-side checks are done by sshd.

questions.text: Which command loads your private key into the running ssh-agent?
questions.explanation: ssh-add asks for the passphrase once and gives the key to the agent. ssh-add -l lists loaded keys. Running ssh-agent FILE would try to run FILE as a command.

questions.text: Which command prints the fingerprint of the key in ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub?
questions.explanation: -l shows the fingerprint and -f names the file. -p changes a key's passphrase, and -R removes a host from known_hosts.

questions.text: What is stored in the client's ~/.ssh/known_hosts file?
options: Public keys of users allowed to log in to this machine
Host keys of servers you have connected to, used to detect impersonation
Hostnames and aliases for your saved connections
A log of past SSH sessions
questions.explanation: On first connection you accept the server's host key, and later connections check it against this file. Aliases belong in ~/.ssh/config, and user keys in authorized_keys.

questions.text: ssh warns REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED! for a server. What is the right first step?
options: Confirm the server's new host-key fingerprint through a trusted channel before trusting it
Generate a new client key with ssh-keygen
questions.explanation: A changed host key may mean a reinstall, or a man-in-the-middle attack. Verify it first; only then remove the old entry with ssh-keygen -R host. Deleting entries or disabling checking removes the protection.

questions.text:
With this block in ~/.ssh/config, what does ssh web do?

Host web
    HostName 203.0.113.10
    User deploy
    Port 2222
options: Looks up a host named web in DNS and connects on port 22
Connects to 203.0.113.10 on port 2222 as user deploy
Connects to 203.0.113.10 on port 22 as your local username
Fails, because Host entries are read only by sshd
questions.explanation: A Host block defines an alias, and the keywords under it apply when you connect to that alias. IdentityFile can also be set there, and -F file points ssh at a different config file.

questions.text: A server was rebuilt, and you have verified its new host key. Which command removes only its old entry from ~/.ssh/known_hosts?
questions.explanation: ssh-keygen -R host deletes that host's keys from known_hosts and keeps a backup. -F only finds and prints the entry, ssh-add -d removes keys from the agent, and deleting the file discards every saved host key.

questions.text: Which file configures the SSH server daemon, as opposed to the client?
questions.explanation: The extra d stands for daemon: sshd_config controls the server, while ssh_config and ~/.ssh/config control the client.

questions.text: Which pair of sshd_config settings blocks direct root logins and allows only key-based logins?
questions.explanation: PermitRootLogin no blocks root over SSH, and PasswordAuthentication no forces key authentication. PubkeyAuthentication no would turn off keys, which is the opposite of what you want.

questions.text: You edited /etc/ssh/sshd_config on a remote server. What is the safest way to apply the change?
options: Run sudo sshd -t, reload the service, and test a new connection before closing the current one
Run sudo systemctl stop ssh, then start it again from the new session
Close your session first, then reconnect to load the new settings
questions.explanation: sshd -t catches syntax errors before they can lock you out. Reloading keeps existing sessions alive, so if the new login fails you can still fix the config from the open session.

questions.text: You changed sshd to listen on port 2222 on a server with UFW. Which firewall step is needed so you can still connect?
questions.explanation: SSH uses TCP, so the new port must be allowed before you rely on it; then remove the old port 22 rule. A non-standard port reduces scan noise but does not replace strong authentication.

questions.text: Which command makes the SSH service start automatically at boot on a Debian-based systemd system?
questions.explanation: enable creates the links that start the unit at boot, and start runs it now. enable --now does both. On many RPM-based systems the unit is named sshd.

questions.text: Which option increases ssh output so you can see where a connection or authentication is failing?
questions.explanation: -v prints debug messages, and -vv or -vvv add more detail. -V prints the version, -q suppresses warnings, and -N skips the remote command.

questions.text: What does ssh -L 8080:localhost:5432 user@db.example.com do?
options: Opens port 8080 on db.example.com and forwards it to port 5432 on your machine
Opens port 8080 on your machine and forwards it through SSH to port 5432 on db.example.com
Starts a SOCKS proxy on local port 8080
Copies the database on port 5432 to local port 8080
questions.explanation: -L local_port:dest_host:dest_port is local forwarding. localhost is resolved on the server side, so connecting to localhost:8080 on your machine reaches the server's local port 5432.

questions.text: Which option creates a reverse tunnel, so that a port on the remote server forwards back to a service on your machine?
questions.explanation: -R remote_port:host:port opens the listening port on the server and sends connections back through the tunnel. -L listens locally, -D starts a SOCKS proxy, and -X forwards X11.

questions.text: What does ssh -D 1080 user@host provide?
options: A debug log written to port 1080
A local SOCKS proxy on port 1080 that sends traffic out through host
A forward from local port 1080 to the same port on host
A disconnect after 1080 seconds of inactivity
questions.explanation: -D sets up dynamic port forwarding. Applications configured to use localhost:1080 as a SOCKS proxy reach any destination as if they were connecting from host.

questions.text: Why add -N to a command such as ssh -N -L 8080:localhost:80 user@host?
options: It disables host-key checking for the tunnel
It keeps the tunnel open without running a remote command or shell
It uses numeric IP addresses only
It compresses traffic through the tunnel
questions.explanation: -N is for forwarding-only sessions. It is often combined with -f to send ssh to the background after authentication. Compression is -C.

questions.text: Which option connects to an internal server through the bastion host jump.example.com in a single command?
questions.explanation: -J (ProxyJump) connects to the jump host first and tunnels the SSH connection to the target through it. In ~/.ssh/config the same thing is written as ProxyJump.

questions.text: What does ssh -X user@host enable?
options: X11 forwarding, so graphical programs on host display on your screen
questions.explanation: -X forwards X11 connections through the encrypted tunnel. The server must allow it with X11Forwarding yes.

questions.text: Which command copies report.pdf from your machine to /srv/docs/ on server?
questions.explanation: scp works like cp: scp SOURCE DEST, with remote paths written as user@host:path. Without the colon, server/srv/docs/ is just a local path.

questions.text: Which command downloads /var/log/app.log from server into the current local directory?
questions.explanation: The remote file is the source, so it comes first, and . (the current directory) is the destination.

questions.text: Which command copies the whole site/ directory to a server whose SSH daemon listens on port 2222?
questions.explanation: scp uses uppercase -P for the port and -r to copy directories. Without -r it refuses to copy a directory, and lowercase -p preserves times and modes.

questions.text: Which scp option preserves the source files' modification times, access times and permission modes?
questions.explanation: Lowercase -p preserves times and modes. -r copies recursively, -C compresses and -q hides the progress meter.

questions.text: Since OpenSSH 9.0, what protocol does the scp command use by default, and how do you force the legacy one?
options: The SCP/rcp protocol; force SFTP with -s
The SFTP protocol; force the legacy SCP protocol with -O
FTP over TLS; force SCP with -T
The rsync protocol; force SCP with -L
questions.explanation: Modern scp sends its transfers over SFTP. The -O flag switches back to the original SCP/rcp protocol for old servers that lack an SFTP subsystem.

questions.text: In an interactive sftp session, which commands upload a local file and download a remote file?
questions.explanation: put local_file uploads to the remote working directory and get remote_file downloads it. ls, cd, mkdir and rm act on the remote side, and exit ends the session.

questions.text: How is SFTP related to SSH?
options: SFTP is FTP with TLS added on top
SFTP runs as a subsystem over an SSH connection, using the same port and authentication
SFTP needs its own daemon listening on port 21
SFTP sends data unencrypted after logging in over SSH
questions.explanation: SFTP is enabled through a Subsystem sftp line in sshd_config. It uses SSH's encryption and logins, typically on port 22. FTP with TLS is FTPS, a different protocol.

questions.text: The server's SSH daemon listens on port 2222. How do you point rsync at it?
questions.explanation: -e sets the remote shell command, so the SSH options go there. In rsync, -P means --partial --progress, not port.

questions.text:
What does this command do?

ssh user@remotehost "tar -czf - /srv/data" > data.tar.gz
options: Copies the local data.tar.gz to the remote host
Creates a compressed archive on the remote host and streams it into a local file
Extracts data.tar.gz into /srv/data on the remote host
Creates data.tar.gz on the remote host and leaves it there
questions.explanation: -f - makes tar write the archive to stdout, ssh carries that stdout back, and the local > saves it. No temporary archive is written on the server.

questions.text: Which plain-text protocol should you avoid on untrusted networks, because it sends logins and data unencrypted?
questions.explanation: Plain FTP sends credentials and files in clear text. SFTP and SCP run over SSH, and FTPS adds TLS encryption to FTP.

questions.text: Which command finds lines containing error, Error or ERROR in app.log?
questions.explanation: -i ignores case. -r recurses into directories, -v inverts the match and -w matches whole words only, all of them still case-sensitive.

questions.text:
app.log has 3 lines, one of which contains error twice. What does grep -c error app.log print?

error: disk full, error: retry failed
ok
error: timeout
questions.explanation: -c counts matching lines, not matches. To count every occurrence, use grep -o error app.log | wc -l, which prints 3 here.

questions.text: What does grep -o change about the output?
options: It prints only the names of matching files
It prints only the matched part of each line, one match per line
It prints only the number of matching lines
It prints only lines that do not match
questions.explanation: -o outputs each matching substring on its own line, which is handy for extracting values such as IP addresses. Filenames only is -l, counts are -c, and inverted matching is -v.

questions.text: Which command shows the active lines of sshd_config, dropping both comment lines and empty lines?
questions.explanation: ^(#|$) matches lines that start with # or are empty, and -v removes them. Without -E, the | is a literal character, and without -v you would print only the lines you wanted to remove.

questions.text: Which command lists the files under src/ that contain main(, printing only their names?
questions.explanation: -r recurses, -l prints only the names of files with a match, and -F treats ( literally. -L lists the files without a match, and -n prints matching lines with line numbers.

questions.text:
Given these lines, which command matches foo and bar foo but not foobar?

foo
foobar
bar foo
questions.explanation: -w requires the match to be a whole word, so foobar is excluded. -x would match only the line that is exactly foo. -F and -i would still match foobar.

questions.text: Which command matches only lines that consist entirely of OK, with nothing else on the line?
questions.explanation: -x anchors the pattern to the whole line, like ^OK$. -w would also match OK fine, because OK is a separate word there.

questions.text: Why does grep 'abc|def' file.txt find nothing, while grep -E 'abc|def' file.txt finds both words?
options: Basic grep needs the pattern in double quotes
In basic regular expressions | is a literal character; -E turns on extended syntax
Basic grep reads only the first line of the file
questions.explanation: In basic regex | is literal. With -E, |, +, ? and () work as operators. You can also use grep -e abc -e def to give several patterns.

questions.text: Which command searches for the literal string 1.2.3.4, so that . does not match any character?
questions.explanation: -F treats the pattern as a fixed string. In every regex mode an unescaped . matches any character, so 1x2y3z4 would also match. You can also escape the dots instead.

questions.text: Which command shows each line containing panic along with the 3 lines that follow it?
questions.explanation: -A means "after" context. -B shows lines before the match, and -C shows lines on both sides.

questions.text: Which command searches only the *.conf files under /etc for Listen?
questions.explanation: --include=GLOB limits a recursive search to files whose base name matches. --exclude does the opposite. Quoting the glob stops the shell from expanding it first.

questions.text: What does sed 's/foo/bar/' input.txt do to the line foo foo foo?
options: Changes it to bar bar bar
Changes it to bar foo foo
Changes it to foo foo bar
Leaves it unchanged unless -i is given
questions.explanation: Without flags, s replaces only the first match on each line. Add g (s/foo/bar/g) to replace every match. Without -i, sed prints the result and leaves the file alone.

questions.text: Which command deletes every line containing DEBUG from app.log in place, keeping a backup as app.log.bak?
questions.explanation: -i.bak edits the file in place after saving the original with a .bak suffix. Redirecting to the same file truncates it before sed reads it, so you lose the data.

questions.text: Which command prints only the lines from START to END, inclusive?
questions.explanation: A /start/,/end/ address selects a range of lines. -n turns off automatic printing, so only p produces output. Without -n, every line prints once and the range prints twice. /START/p;/END/p prints only the two marker lines.

questions.text: Which command deletes all empty lines from file.txt, printing the result?
questions.explanation: ^$ matches a line with nothing between the start and the end, and d deletes it. s/^$// replaces nothing with nothing, so the empty lines stay. /$/ matches every line.

questions.text: Which command inserts a line # generated before the first line of config.ini, writing the result to stdout?
questions.explanation: i\ inserts text before the addressed line, a\ appends after it, and c\ replaces it. Address 1 is the first line and $ is the last.

questions.text:
What does this sed command with capture groups print?

echo 'user=alice' | sed -E 's/(.*)=(.*)/\2=\1/'
questions.explanation: With -E, parentheses are capture groups, and \1 and \2 in the replacement refer back to them. Without -E you would write \(.*\)=\(.*\).

questions.text: Which command removes the third character from every line?
questions.explanation: ^(..). captures the first two characters and matches the third, then \1 puts back only the two. In basic regex, {3} must be written \{3\}, and y translates characters rather than deleting them.

questions.text: Which awk command prints the username (field 1) and UID (field 3) from /etc/passwd?
questions.explanation: /etc/passwd is colon-separated, so set the field separator with -F:. By default awk splits on runs of whitespace. The action must be inside braces.

questions.text: What does awk '{ print NF, $NF }' print for the line a b c d?
questions.explanation: NF is the number of fields in the current line, and $NF is the last field. NR would be the line (record) number.

questions.text: Which command prints the total of the numbers in column 2 of sales.txt?
questions.explanation: The main block runs for every line, adding up $2, and END runs once after the last line. The first option prints a running total on every line, and BEGIN runs before any input is read.

questions.text: Which command prints the names of users whose UID is 1000 or higher?
questions.explanation: A condition before the action limits which lines it runs on. > 1000 would leave out UID 1000 itself, and /1000/ matches the text 1000 anywhere in the line.

questions.text: Which command prints x,z for the input x:y:z?
questions.explanation: -F: splits the input on colons, and OFS is the output field separator that print places between comma-separated items. RS is the record separator, and $1 $3 joins the fields with nothing in between.

questions.text: Which command counts how often each value in column 1 of access.log appears?
options: awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}' access.log
questions.explanation: c[$1]++ uses an associative array keyed by the first field, and the END loop prints each key with its count. The order of for (k in c) is unspecified, so pipe the output to sort if needed.

questions.text: What does sort numbers.txt output for lines 10, 9 and 100?
questions.explanation: Without options, sort compares lines as text, character by character, so 1… sorts before 9. Use sort -n to compare numerically and get 9, 10, 100.

questions.text: Which command sorts scores.txt numerically by its second column, highest first?
questions.explanation: -k2 sorts on the second field, -n compares numbers and -r reverses the order. -t sets the field delimiter, not the key.

questions.text: Why does uniq usually appear after sort in a pipeline?
options: uniq only works on numeric data
uniq removes only adjacent duplicate lines
uniq reverses the order of its input
sort adds the line numbers that uniq needs
questions.explanation: uniq compares each line with the one before it. Sorting first puts identical lines next to each other, so printf 'b a b ' | uniq keeps all three lines. sort -u does both steps at once.

questions.text: Which pipeline lists the most frequent lines in ips.txt first, each with its count?
questions.explanation: sort groups duplicates, uniq -c prefixes each distinct line with its count, and sort -rn puts the biggest counts first. uniq -d prints only the duplicated lines, without counts.

questions.text: Which command prints the usernames (the first colon-separated field) from /etc/passwd?
questions.explanation: -d: sets the delimiter and -f1 picks the first field. Without -d, cut splits on tabs, and -c1 would print only the first character.

questions.text: Which command turns hello world into HELLO WORLD?
questions.explanation: tr SET1 SET2 maps each character in the first set to the matching one in the second. 'a-z' 'A-Z' also works for ASCII text. -d deletes characters and -s squeezes repeats.

questions.text: What does echo 'a1b2c3' | tr -d '0-9' print?
questions.explanation: tr -d deletes every character in the given set, here the digits, leaving abc.

questions.text: Which command counts the lines in access.log?
questions.explanation: -l counts newline characters, which is the number of lines. -w counts words, -c bytes and -m characters.

questions.text: Which command finds regular files larger than 100 MiB under the current directory?
questions.explanation: +N means more than N, -N means less than N, and a bare N means exactly N (rounded up to whole units). A bare number with no suffix counts 512-byte blocks.

questions.text: Which command lists only the directories under /usr/local?
questions.explanation: -type d matches directories, f regular files and l symbolic links. -name d matches entries literally named d.

questions.text: Which command finds files under /home that are not owned by guest?
questions.explanation: ! (or -not) negates the test that follows it. -user !guest would look for a user literally named !guest.

questions.text: What is the difference between -exec rm -- {} \; and -exec rm -- {} + in find?
options: \; deletes directories and + deletes only files
\; runs rm once per file, while + passes many files to each rm
+ asks before each deletion, while \; does not
\; is for GNU find only, while + works everywhere
questions.explanation: {} + batches pathnames like xargs, creating far fewer processes. Both forms handle spaces in names safely. Asking before each command is what -ok does.

questions.text: Which find action asks for confirmation before running the command on each match?
questions.explanation: -ok works like -exec but prompts before each command, which is a safer way to delete. -delete removes matches without asking.

questions.text: Which command uses the locate database to find paths containing readme, whether written README, Readme or readme?
questions.explanation: -i ignores case. -l N limits the number of results and -S prints database statistics. locate searches a prebuilt database, so run sudo updatedb first if files are very new.

questions.text: which ls prints /usr/bin/ls, but typing ls runs ls --color=auto. Which command shows the alias as well as the files on PATH?
questions.explanation: type is a Bash builtin that reports aliases, functions, builtins and files on PATH, in the order the shell resolves them. An external which searches only PATH.

questions.text:
What does this xargs -n 2 pipeline print?

printf '%s\n' one two three four five | xargs -n 2 echo
options: one two three four five on one line
one two, three four, then five on separate lines
Each word on its own line
questions.explanation: -n 2 passes at most two arguments to each echo, so echo runs three times. Without -n, xargs puts as many arguments as fit into a single command.

questions.text: Which pipeline safely deletes every *.tmp file, even when names contain spaces or newlines?
questions.explanation: -print0 ends each pathname with a NUL byte, and xargs -0 splits only on NUL, so whitespace stays part of the name. By default xargs splits on blanks, so a b.tmp becomes two bad arguments.

questions.text: In xargs rm --, which program is the -- for, and why is it there?
options: It is for xargs, telling it to read NUL-separated input
It is for rm, so that file names starting with - are not read as options
It is for the shell, to end the pipeline
It is for rm, to make it delete directories recursively
questions.explanation: xargs adds the input items after rm --, and -- tells rm that everything after it is a filename. Without it, a file named -rf would be read as options.

questions.text: Which command runs gzip on each listed file, with up to 4 compressions running at once?
questions.explanation: -P 4 allows four parallel processes, and -n 1 gives each gzip a single file. -n 4 alone runs gzip with four files at a time, one invocation after another.

questions.text: What does printf '%s\n' web1 web2 | xargs -I {} ssh {} uptime do?
options: Runs a single ssh with both hostnames as arguments
Runs ssh web1 uptime, then ssh web2 uptime
Runs ssh in parallel on both hosts
Prints the commands without running them
questions.explanation: -I {} swaps each input line in for {} and runs one command per item. Parallelism needs -P, and printing each command as it runs needs -t.

questions.text: On GNU systems, find . -name '*.bak' -print0 | xargs -0 rm -- finds no files. How do you stop rm from running at all in that case?
questions.explanation: GNU xargs normally runs the command once even with empty input; -r (--no-run-if-empty) skips it. -r is not in POSIX, so find ... -exec rm -- {} + is the portable alternative.

questions.text: Which command creates a gzip-compressed archive project.tar.gz from the directory project/?
questions.explanation: -c creates, -z compresses through gzip and -f names the archive. -x extracts and -t lists. gzip -r compresses each file separately and makes no archive.

questions.text: Why does tar -cfz backup.tar.gz project/ not create a compressed backup.tar.gz?
options: -z must always come before -c
-f takes the next text, z, as the archive name, so backup.tar.gz is read as a file to add
tar refuses to create files with a .gz extension
-cfz creates a bzip2 archive instead
questions.explanation: -f needs an argument, and in a bundled option group it takes the rest of the group. Keep f last, as in -czf backup.tar.gz project/.

questions.text: How do you list the contents of backup.tar.gz without extracting anything?
questions.explanation: -t lists the archive's members, and with -v it shows permissions, owner, size and date like ls -l. gzip -d would decompress the file into backup.tar.

questions.text: Which command extracts project.tar.gz into /opt/restore instead of the current directory?
questions.explanation: -C DIR makes tar change into that directory before extracting. Redirecting stdout does not move the extracted files, and -c would create an archive instead.

questions.text: Which command extracts only docs/readme.txt from archive.tar.gz?
questions.explanation: Member names given after the archive limit extraction to those paths, which must match how they appear in tar -tzf. The archive name must come straight after -f.

questions.text: Which command archives app/ but leaves out its app/tmp/ contents?
questions.explanation: In GNU tar, --exclude is position-sensitive and must come before the file operands it applies to. The quotes stop the shell from expanding the pattern. -x means extract.

questions.text: Which tar option compresses with xz, as in archive.tar.xz?
questions.explanation: -z is gzip (.tar.gz), -j is bzip2 (.tar.bz2) and capital -J is xz (.tar.xz). Lowercase -x means extract.

questions.text: You need to split big.tar into 100 MB pieces for upload, then rebuild it later. Which pair of commands works?
options: split -b 100M big.tar part_, then cat part_* > big.tar
split -l 100 big.tar part_, then tar -xf part_*
questions.explanation: split -b cuts the file into byte-sized chunks named part_aa, part_ab and so on. The glob expands in sorted order, so cat puts them back together correctly. -l splits by lines.

questions.text: Which command compresses log.txt to log.txt.gz but also keeps the original file?
questions.explanation: By default gzip replaces the file with the .gz version. -k keeps the original, -d decompresses and -l lists compression statistics.

questions.text: Which crontab line runs /opt/backup.sh at 7:30 AM, Monday to Friday?
questions.explanation: The five fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. 1-5 in the fifth field means Monday to Friday; in the third field it would mean the 1st to the 5th of the month.

questions.text: When does the crontab entry */15 * * * * /opt/check.sh run?
options: 15 minutes after cron starts, then every 15 minutes from that point
At minutes 0, 15, 30 and 45 of every hour
Once at 15 minutes past each hour
questions.explanation: Cron schedules are calendar matches, not timers. */15 in the minute field is a step value that matches minutes divisible by 15. 15 alone would run once an hour at minute 15.

questions.text: A cron job 0 2 * * * tar -czf /backup/$(date +%F).tar.gz /data never produces a correctly named file. Why?
options: An unescaped % is special in crontab commands and must be written as \%
$(...) is not allowed in cron jobs
Cron jobs cannot write to /backup
questions.explanation: Cron treats % as a newline, and text after the first % is sent to the command's stdin. Write date +\%F, or move the logic into a script.

questions.text: How do lines in /etc/crontab differ from lines you add with crontab -e?
options: They have an extra username field between the time fields and the command
They use seconds as the first field
They must use full month names
questions.explanation: System crontabs (/etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d/) say which user runs each job. User crontabs already belong to one user, so they have only the five time fields and the command.

questions.text: A laptop is often off at night, and you want a daily job to still run once it boots. Which tool suits this better than plain cron?
questions.explanation: Plain cron skips jobs whose time passes while the machine is off. anacron tracks when each periodic job last ran and catches up after boot, which suits machines that are not always on.

questions.text: Which file lists local user accounts with their UID, home directory and login shell?
questions.explanation: Each line of /etc/passwd describes one account: name, password placeholder, UID, primary GID, comment, home directory and shell. Password hashes live in /etc/shadow.

questions.text: Which file stores the password hashes and password-aging data for local accounts?
questions.explanation: /etc/shadow holds salted one-way hashes plus expiry fields and is readable only by root. /etc/passwd is world-readable, so it only contains an x placeholder.

questions.text:
What does this /etc/passwd line tell you about the account?

deploy:x:1001:2000:Deploy User:/srv/deploy:/usr/sbin/nologin
options: UID 1001, primary GID 2000, home /srv/deploy, and no interactive login shell
UID 2000, primary GID 1001, home /srv/deploy, and the password is x
UID 1001, primary GID 2000, and the password stored in plain text in field 2
questions.explanation: The fields are name, password placeholder (x means "see /etc/shadow"), UID, primary GID, comment, home and shell. A shell of nologin is typical for service accounts.

questions.text: In /etc/shadow, what does a password field that starts with ! mean?
options: The account has no password and anyone can log in
The password must be changed at next login
Password authentication is disabled for the account
questions.explanation: A hash prefixed with ! (or a field of *) cannot match any password, so password logins fail. passwd -l locks accounts this way, but other methods such as SSH keys may still work.

questions.text: Which command creates the user adam together with a home directory?
questions.explanation: -m creates the home directory and copies the skeleton files into it. Without it, whether a home is created depends on distribution defaults; -M explicitly skips it.

questions.text: Which command creates the user alice without a home directory, even if the system default would create one?
questions.explanation: -M (--no-create-home) overrides CREATE_HOME in /etc/login.defs. usermod changes existing accounts, and passwd -d deletes a password.

questions.text: How do useradd and adduser differ?
options: adduser can only create system accounts
adduser is a friendlier, interactive front end that is not available on every distribution
useradd always prompts for the full name and password
useradd only works on Red Hat systems
questions.explanation: adduser asks questions and sets up the home directory for you, but it may be missing or behave differently across distributions. useradd is the low-level tool and the safer choice in portable scripts.

questions.text: Which command adds the existing user bob to the supplementary group docker without removing his other groups?
questions.explanation: -a appends to the supplementary group list. useradd would try to create a new user, and groupadd creates groups rather than adding members.

questions.text: What happens if you run usermod -G docker bob without -a?
options: Bob is added to docker and keeps his other groups
Bob's primary group changes to docker
The command fails because -a is mandatory
Bob's supplementary groups are replaced, so he is removed from any group other than docker
questions.explanation: Without -a, -G sets the complete list of supplementary groups. Forgetting -a is a classic way to accidentally remove someone from sudo or wheel.

questions.text: Which command removes user adam from the group admins?
questions.explanation: gpasswd -d deletes a single member from a group. groupdel removes the whole group and userdel deletes the user account.

questions.text: A line in /etc/group reads admins:x:1001:adam,eve. What does 1001 represent?
questions.explanation: The fields are group name, password placeholder, GID and a comma-separated member list. getent group admins prints the same format.

questions.text: What does id adam display?
options: Adam's UID, primary GID and group memberships
questions.explanation: id prints something like uid=1000(adam) gid=1000(adam) groups=1000(adam),27(sudo). Expiry details come from chage -l and logins from last.

questions.text: Which command changes the login shell of user carol to /bin/zsh?
questions.explanation: chsh -s updates the shell field in /etc/passwd (as does usermod -s). useradd creates new accounts, and exporting SHELL only affects the current session.

questions.text: Which command locks the password of user dave so password logins fail?
questions.explanation: -l prefixes the hash with !. It does not disable the account entirely, so SSH key logins may still work. -d removes the password, -e forces a change at next login and -S shows status.

questions.text: Which command deletes the user eve together with her home directory and mail spool?
questions.explanation: -r removes the home directory and mail spool along with the account. Plain userdel leaves the files behind, and deleting the directory alone leaves the account in place.

questions.text: What UID does the root account have?
questions.explanation: The kernel grants superuser privileges to UID 0, whatever the account is called. Regular users usually start at 1000, and 65534 is commonly nobody.

questions.text: What is the difference between su adam and su - adam?
options: su - adam does not ask for a password
su adam switches to root first
su - adam starts a login shell with adam's own environment and startup files
su - adam runs only one command and then exits
questions.explanation: The - (or -l) option simulates a full login: adam's environment variables are loaded and you start in his home directory. Plain su adam keeps much of the caller's environment.

questions.text: Which command runs whoami as user adam and then returns to your own session?
questions.explanation: su -c passes a single command to the target user's shell, and the output appears in your terminal. Here it prints adam.

questions.text: To give user adam administrative rights through the default sudoers setup, which group do you add him to on Debian/Ubuntu versus RHEL/Fedora?
options: sudo on Debian/Ubuntu and wheel on RHEL/Fedora
wheel on Debian/Ubuntu and sudo on RHEL/Fedora
questions.explanation: Debian-based systems grant %sudo full rights, while Red Hat-based systems use %wheel. For example, usermod -aG wheel adam on RHEL.

questions.text: Why should you edit /etc/sudoers with visudo rather than a regular editor?
options: Regular editors cannot open files in /etc
visudo locks the file and checks the syntax before saving, preventing a broken configuration
visudo automatically grants the current user full rights
questions.explanation: A syntax error in sudoers can stop sudo from working at all, locking you out of administration. visudo validates the file and refuses to install a broken version.

questions.text: What does the sudoers line %wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL do?
options: Grants the user named wheel full sudo rights
Lets all members of the wheel group run any command as any user on any host
Lets all users run commands as members of the wheel group
Denies the wheel group any sudo rights
questions.explanation: % marks a group. The fields are hosts (ALL), the users you may become ((ALL)) and the allowed commands (ALL). By default users still have to enter their own password.

questions.text: What does the sudoers line adam ALL = NOPASSWD:/sbin/reboot allow?
options: Adam can run any command without a password
Adam can reboot only after entering the root password
Every user can reboot without a password
Adam can run /sbin/reboot through sudo without being asked for a password
questions.explanation: The rule names one user and one command, and the NOPASSWD: tag skips authentication for it. Other commands still follow the remaining rules.

questions.text: Which sudoers line lets user alice run only /usr/bin/systemctl as root, still asking for her password?
questions.explanation: Listing one command restricts alice to it, and without NOPASSWD: she must authenticate. ALL would allow every command, and ! would forbid systemctl instead.

questions.text: What does sudo -l show?
options: All processes currently running as root
Which commands the invoking user may run with sudo on this host
The list of members in the sudo group
questions.explanation: sudo -l (list) prints the user's allowed and forbidden commands according to the sudoers policy. It is the quickest way to check what a new rule grants.

questions.text: Which sudo option starts a login shell as the target user, reading that user's profile files?
questions.explanation: sudo -i runs the target user's shell as a login shell, much like su -. -E preserves your environment, -l lists privileges and -u only chooses the target user.

questions.text: Which command runs make install as root while asking sudo to keep your current environment variables?
questions.explanation: -E (--preserve-env) requests that your environment be kept, if the security policy allows it. -i uses a login environment and -k discards cached credentials.

questions.text: Which sudoers Defaults setting makes commands run with a minimal, clean environment instead of the caller's variables?
questions.explanation: env_reset (on by default) discards most of the caller's environment. env_keep lists exceptions that are kept, and secure_path sets the PATH used for commands.

questions.text: What does the execute (x) permission mean on a directory?
options: Programs in the directory can be run
Files can be created in the directory
The directory's file names can be listed
The directory can be entered and traversed to reach entries inside it
questions.explanation: For directories, r lists names, w lets you create, delete and rename entries (together with x), and x allows access through the directory. Without x, cd and opening files inside fail.

questions.text: Bob has write and execute permission on /shared, which has no sticky bit. A file there is owned by alice with mode 444. Can bob delete it?
options: No, because the file is read-only
No, because only the owner can delete a file
Yes, because deleting a file needs write and execute permission on the directory, not on the file
Yes, but only if bob is in alice's group
questions.explanation: Removing a file removes a directory entry, so the directory's permissions decide. rm may ask about a write-protected file, but it succeeds. The sticky bit is what prevents this in shared directories.

questions.text: Which symbolic permissions does octal mode 754 represent?
questions.explanation: Each digit is the sum of read 4, write 2 and execute 1: 7 = rwx for the owner, 5 = r-x for the group and 4 = r-- for others.

questions.text: Which octal mode does chmod u=rw,go=r file.txt set?
questions.explanation: u=rw gives the owner 6 and go=r gives group and others 4 each. The = operator sets the permissions exactly rather than adding to them.

questions.text: What is the effect of chmod o-rwx file.txt?
options: It grants all permissions to others
It removes all permissions for the owner
It removes read, write and execute permission for others, leaving owner and group unchanged
questions.explanation: o selects others and - removes the listed bits. Owner (u) and group (g) permissions are not touched.

questions.text: With umask 027, what permissions does a new regular file get when the program requests mode 666?
questions.explanation: The umask clears bits: 666 with group write and all of others' bits masked gives 640. Directories requested as 777 would become 750.

questions.text: Why can ordinary users change their own password even though /etc/shadow is writable only by root?
options: /etc/shadow has the sticky bit set
Users are temporarily added to the root group
/usr/bin/passwd is setuid root, so it runs with the file owner's privileges
Password changes are written to the user's home directory
questions.explanation: The setuid bit makes an executable run with its owner's user ID. Because setuid programs run as root, they must be audited carefully.

questions.text: ls -l shows -rwSr--r-- for a file. What does the uppercase S mean?
options: The file has the sticky bit
The setuid bit is set, but the owner has no execute permission
The file is a symbolic link
questions.explanation: A lowercase s means setuid plus execute, while S means the special bit is present without the underlying x, which usually signals a mistake.

questions.text: Which permission on a shared project directory makes new files inherit the directory's group?
questions.explanation: With setgid on a directory, new files get the directory's group and new subdirectories inherit setgid. It does not grant group write; use a suitable umask or a default ACL for that.

questions.text: What does the sticky bit do on a world-writable directory such as /tmp?
options: It makes every file in the directory executable
It prevents anyone from deleting files
It lets only a file's owner, the directory's owner or root delete or rename that file
It clears the directory at every reboot
questions.explanation: Without the sticky bit, anyone with write permission on the directory could remove other users' files. ls -ld /tmp shows it as a t in the last position (drwxrwxrwt).

questions.text: Which command lists every file on the system that has the setuid bit set?
questions.explanation: In octal, 4000 is setuid, 2000 is setgid and 1000 is the sticky bit. -perm /4000 matches files with that bit set; 2>/dev/null hides permission errors.

questions.text: Which command recursively sets mode 755 on every directory under project/ without changing regular files?
